a: the start of the year
t: "The start of the year" or "the first month"?
p: The Hebrew says "at the head of the year". The Greek says "in the first month".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: the start of the year
readings.plain: the start of the year

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: in the first month
readings.plain: in the first month

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Hebrew b'rosh hashanah ("at the head of the year") is the only place in the Bible where this phrase is used for a date. The Greek explains it as the first month, spring, which is how Ezekiel counts in 45:18, 21 and in the Passover calendar.

a: To the south
p: The Hebrew mineged is read "to the south"; the Greek reads "opposite".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: To the south
readings.plain: To the south

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: Opposite
readings.plain: Opposite

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Hebrew word min-neged can mean "from the south" (as in the Negev, the south) or "opposite". The Greek has apenanti, "opposite". The Plain takes "south" because the city lies south of the Temple in 48:15-17.

a: He measured the porch of the gate on the side toward the house: one reed.
t: Verse 8: the porch again, or a third chamber?
p: The Hebrew repeats the porch measure. The Greek has a measurement of the third chamber.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: He measured the porch of the gate on the side toward the house: one reed.
readings.plain: He measured the porch of the gate on the side toward the house: one reed.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: The third chamber was also one reed wide and one reed long.
readings.plain: The third chamber was also one reed wide and one reed long.

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Hebrew 40:8 repeats the end of 40:7, and a scribe's eye may have skipped or doubled the line. The Greek has a different text in 40:6-9 and reads here that "the third chamber" measured a reed each way, which fits a gate with three chambers a side. The Greek could be right, or it could be the translator's own way of making sense of a text he found hard.

a: sixty cubits
p: The Hebrew says sixty. The Greek says twenty. Neither fits well.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: sixty cubits
readings.plain: sixty cubits

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: twenty cubits
readings.plain: twenty cubits

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text. The verse is also uncertain in its other words (see the note).
b: Sixty cubits does not fit beside a gate that is 50 long and 25 wide. Twenty, which is what the Greek has, would possibly fit the width of the passage if the porch is meant (compare 40:49). The Plain keeps the Masoretic reading and flags the problem.

a: Porches ran all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide.
p: The Hebrew has this verse. The Greek (in Swete's text) has no verse 30.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: Porches ran all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide.
readings.plain: Porches ran all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. Swete's Greek has no text for this verse, and that may be a copying or translating slip rather than a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to leave the verse out.
b: The verse is awkward in the Hebrew: "twenty-five by five" does not match the porch of 40:9, 15 or 49, and the matching verses for the other gates have no equivalent. One explanation for the Greek is that an eye jumped from the end of 40:29 ("twenty-five cubits") to the end of 40:30 ("twenty-five cubits"). Another is that the verse was added to the Hebrew later. The evidence read here does not choose between them. Swete's numbering leaves an empty slot at 40:30.

a: Its porches opened toward the outer courtyard.
p: The Hebrew has the porches of the east inner gate facing the outer courtyard. The Greek has them facing the inner courtyard.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: Its porches opened toward the outer courtyard.
readings.plain: Its porches opened toward the outer courtyard.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: αἰλαμμὼν εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν τὴν ἐσωτέραν
readings.en: Its porches opened toward the inner courtyard.
readings.plain: Its porches opened toward the inner courtyard.

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: Every other inner gate in the Hebrew has its porch toward the outer courtyard (40:31, 37), and so do the Greek's other two (Swete's 40:31 and 40:37). Only the Greek of 40:34 differs. It may be a slip, or a different Hebrew word; the evidence is thin.

a: the sin offering and the guilt offering
p: The Hebrew names the sin offering and the guilt offering. The Greek names the sin offering and the offering for sins of ignorance.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse

readings.plain: the sin offering and the guilt offering

readings.orig: τὰ ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτίας καὶ ὑπὲρ ἀγνοίας
readings.en: the offerings for sin and for sins of ignorance
readings.plain: the offerings for sin and for sins of ignorance

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: In the Greek, the clause reads "so that they may slaughter in it the offerings for sin and for ignorance"; it has no burnt offering. "Ignorance" may be the Greek's wording for the guilt offering, since the guilt offering of Leviticus 5 deals with sin done unknowingly (Leviticus 5:15, 18).

a: rooms for singers
t: Rooms for singers, or just two rooms?
p: The Hebrew calls the two rooms "rooms for singers". The Greek has "two rooms" and no word for singers.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: rooms for singers
readings.plain: rooms for singers

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: two rooms
readings.plain: two rooms

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which has the word. The Greek has no counterpart, and 40:45-46 give the same two rooms to the priests, so the verse makes sense without singers.
b: Levite singers are well known in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah, but this is the only place in Ezekiel's Temple where the Hebrew puts them. Whether the Hebrew word was added or the Greek dropped it cannot be settled from the evidence read here. The note at this verse and the topic on the Temple singers say the same.

a: The other stood at the side of the east gate, facing north.
p: The Hebrew puts the second room by the east gate. The Greek puts it by the south gate.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: The other stood at the side of the east gate, facing north.
readings.plain: The other stood at the side of the east gate, facing north.

readings.en: The other stood at the side of the south gate, facing north.
readings.plain: The other stood at the side of the south gate, facing north.

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which is the only Hebrew witness, but the Greek makes a neater plan.
b: With two rooms facing each other across the inner court, one at the north gate looking south and one at the south gate looking north, the plan is symmetrical, as in the Greek. The Hebrew "east gate" breaks that pattern. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and gives this variant.

a: The width of the gate was three cubits on this side and three on that.
p: The Hebrew gives only "three and three" for the gate of the porch. The Greek adds a doorway of fourteen cubits, and has the "three and three" as the doorway's sides.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.orig: וְרֹחַב הַשַּׁעַר שָׁלֹשׁ אַמּוֹת מִפֹּו וְשָׁלֹשׁ אַמּוֹת מִפֹּו
readings.en: The width of the gate was three cubits on this side and three on that.
readings.plain: The width of the gate was three cubits on this side and three on that.

readings.plain: the width of the doorway fourteen cubits, and the sides of the doorway three cubits on this side and three on that

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Greek's fourteen has no counterpart in the Hebrew. The Greek of 40:48 also calls the porch pillars by a transliterated word (ail) and the porch by ailam, as the Hebrew 'ayil and 'ulam, which suggests a translator working from a Hebrew text close to ours. Why the number was added is not known.

a: eleven cubits wide
p: The Hebrew has "eleven" (literally "one and ten"). The Greek has twelve.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse

readings.plain: eleven cubits wide

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: twelve cubits wide
readings.plain: twelve cubits wide

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Greek of 40:49 also says people went up to the porch by ten steps, a number that the Hebrew does not give (it says only "the steps"). The Hebrew "one and ten" is an unusual way to say eleven. Which number is original is not clear.

a: That was the width of the tent.
p: The Hebrew says "tent". The Greek has "porch" and measures the porch.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: That was the width of the tent.
readings.plain: That was the width of the tent.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: That was the width of the porch.
readings.plain: That was the width of the porch.

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Hebrew 'ohel and 'ulam look alike. In the Greek of 41:1-2 the pillars are not mentioned and the porch is measured on each side, then the doorway, so the whole verse is smoother. The Hebrew is the harder reading, which in textual criticism is often the original, so the Plain keeps it.

a: The entrance was six cubits, and the width of the entrance was seven cubits.
t: Seven cubits wide, or seven on each side?
p: The Hebrew gives the entrance a width of seven cubits. The Greek makes seven the thickness of each side of the doorway, and has the guide go into "the inner court". The Qumran copy agrees with the Hebrew where it is preserved.

readings.plain: The entrance was six cubits, and the width of the entrance was seven cubits.

readings.orig: איל הפתח שתים אמות והפתח שש אמות [ורחב] הפתח שבע [אמות]

readings.plain: he went into the inner court … the sides of the doorway seven cubits on this side and seven on that

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, with 4QEzek-a (4Q73) agreeing in the words that are preserved. The Greek's "inner court" and its seven on each side are a different reading of the same line.
b: The scroll is a fragment: the words before "the pillar" and the word "width" are brackets, restored by the editors, so only the measures themselves are the scroll's own. They match the Hebrew. The Greek may be reading lifnimah ("inward") as a noun, "the inner (court)", and spreading the seven cubits to both sides of the door.

a: its length, twenty cubits
p: The Hebrew and the Qumran copy give the innermost room a length of twenty cubits. The Greek gives forty.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), with 4QEzek-a (4Q73)

readings.plain: its length, twenty cubits

readings.plain: the length of the doors, forty cubits

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, and a Dead Sea copy has the same number, so the Greek's forty is not the reading of every early Hebrew copy.
b: 4QEzek-a (4Q73) preserves "its length, twenty cubits" and then "width [twenty] cubits" with only the second "twenty" restored. So a Qumran scroll sides with the Masoretic Text against the Greek on the size of the innermost room. Forty is the length of the great hall in 41:2 in both texts, which may have crept into the Greek here, but that is a guess. Twenty fits the cube of the innermost room (1 Kings 6:20).

a: thirty-three times
t: "Three and thirty times" and the Greek count
p: The Hebrew and the Qumran copy read "three and thirty times". The Greek reads "thirty, three times, twice".

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text, which 4QEzek-a (4Q73) shares word for word here.
b: 4Q73 has the Hebrew count in full (the word before it and the word after it are restored, but the count itself is not). The Greek is a literal-sounding string that does not clearly give a number. The note at this verse sets out the two ways the Hebrew can be read.

p: The Hebrew breaks off. The Greek carries it into verse 22 ("like the appearance of an altar of wood"). This entry and the next go together.

readings.plain: the appearance was like the appearance

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The Hebrew ends 41:21 with "the appearance like the appearance", and then 41:22 starts "the altar was wood". The Greek joins the two: "...an appearance like the appearance of an altar of wood". That would make 41:22 describe what stands before the holy place. The Greek is the smoother reading, and the Hebrew is hard; the Plain follows the Hebrew.

p: This goes with the previous entry. In the Greek the sentence runs on from 41:21.

b: See the entry at 41:21. The Greek of 41:22 begins "of an altar of wood" and carries on with its measurements, and it adds "and it had horns".

a: five hundred reeds
p: The Hebrew counts "five hundred reeds" on each side. The Greek gives no unit in three of the four verses. These four entries go together.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); no Qumran scroll preserves this verse
readings.en: five hundred reeds
readings.plain: five hundred reeds

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.orig: πεντακοσίους ἐν τῷ καλάμῳ τοῦ μέτρου
readings.en: five hundred, by the measuring reed
readings.plain: five hundred, by the measuring reed

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text and its unusual count. The Qere at 42:16 reads "hundreds" (me'ot) where the Ketiv has the letters of 'amot, "cubits"; the two words are the same four letters in a different order, so the note corrects a spelling and does not ask whether reeds or cubits is meant.
b: Five hundred reeds is 3,000 cubits, about a mile; five hundred cubits is about 850 feet. The Hebrew of 42:20 gives 500 by 500 and 45:2 gives 500 by 500, each with no unit; cubits is what the Greek says at 42:17 and in the second half of 42:20. The Mishnah gives the Second Temple's mount as 500 cubits (Middot 2:1). In the Greek, 42:16, 18 and 19 read "five hundred, by the measuring reed" with no unit, and only 42:17 reads "five hundred cubits". The Greek also lists the sides in a different order: east, north, west ("the sea"), south, where the Hebrew has east, north, south, west. The Hebrew may be corrupt or may use "reed" loosely, but the Plain keeps the text it has and gives the other reading.

b: The Hebrew leshachat, "to destroy", is the verb of the destroyer in Exodus 12:23 and of the executioners of chapter 9. The Greek chrisai, "to anoint", looks like a different Hebrew verb (limshoach) or a deliberate softening. Both the Hebrew pointing and the Greek ("I was entering") have the first person, "I".

The word for "leaders" (hegoumenoi) is not the usual Greek for "kings". See the note at this verse for the readings of the Hebrew.

b: The Hebrew 'azarah here is a rare word for a ledge or border of the altar, and the Greek translator chose hilasterion, the word of Exodus 25:17-22 for the ark's cover, the mercy seat. It is the word of Hebrews 9:5 and Romans 3:25. The note at 43:14 says what this does and does not show.

p: The Hebrew has "four" after "the horns"; the Greek has "a cubit".

b: In the Hebrew haqqeranot arba' can mean "the horns, four", which fits the four corners (43:20). The Greek has pechys, "cubit", which would make the horns a cubit tall. The Masoretic Text has the four-horns reading, which agrees with the altar of Exodus 27:2.

readings.w: Greek (Septuagint), as printed in Swete's text of Codex Vaticanus
readings.en: they will fill their hands
readings.plain: they will fill their hands

why: The Plain follows the Masoretic Text. The Greek here is one witness against it, and it may be a translator's smoothing or a different Hebrew text; the evidence is not strong enough to change the base text.
b: The idiom "fill the hand" is used of installing priests (Exodus 29:9, 33). The Hebrew has the altar as the one whose hand is filled, by the written "its hand" and the read "its hands". The Greek makes the priests the ones installed. The two readings may be one idea: the altar is put in service by priests who are themselves put in service.
